newsitem.title: FRANCE: French privatisation stocks dive on left poll win.
newsitem.headline: French privatisation stocks dive on left poll win.

text.p: Shares in French companies slated for privatisation plunged on Monday after the election victory of the Socialist-led left cast doubt over the outgoing government's sale plans.
The Socialists refused to comment on Monday morning on the planned sale of a stake in France Telecom, which had the highest profile of the outgoing government's privatisation projects.

"I am not saying no comment and I am not denying anything," a party spokesman told Reuters when asked about a rumour that the newly-elected left had cancelled the privatisation. "There is no government, so there is no decision," he added.
A spokesman at France Telecom said the operator had no comment.

A decision on whether to proceed with the France Telecom sale is eagerly awaited by financial markets and international investors because it would be seen to set the tone for other planned privatisations.
The Socialists are to hold a meeting at their headquarters at 1300 GMT and plan a news conference to follow but it was not clear whether any immediate decisions on asset sales would be announced.
Shares in Thomson-CSF, also set for privatisation this month by the outgoing government, were down 7.48 percent at 152.20 francs on prospects its sale could be delayed or scrapped.
The Socialists were silent on the outlook for this sale.
Stocks in conglomerate Lagardere and engineering firm Alcatel Alsthom, the two rivals in the bidding war over Thomson-CSF, were down sharply.

At 1040 GMT, Lagardere stock was down 6.65 percent at 158.50 francs, while Alcatel was off 3.36 percent at 604 francs. Shares in Dassault Aviation, the combat plane maker bidding jointly with Alcatel for Thomson-CSF, were suspended limit down at 981 francs.
Trade in investment certificates of troubled bank Credit Lyonnais were also much lower, down 5.79 percent at 203.50 francs.
The Paris CAC-40 stock index was down 1.41 percent, well off its lows from earlier in the day.
The Socialists, who said early in the campaign they would cancel the sale of France Telecom and other planned privatisations, later backed off.
Late last week, party leader Lionel Jospin said the government would consult the staff of France Telecom and that their wishes would be a factor in decisions.
The Communists, who hold the balance of power alongside the dominant Socialist party in the National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, oppose privatisations.
They were planning a news conference later on Monday at which they were expected to list some conditions for joining a Socialist-led government.
Most analysts said before the election that the Socialists might be forced into the sale of minority stakes in state-owned companies to pay for other economic policies.

The Socialists promised, among other things, to create 700,000 new jobs for the young, with half in the public sector, and to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay -- both potentially expensive pledges.
